summary: Registers the Enumservice vCard, using http and https URIs, so that an ENUM domain name for a phone number can point to a vCard describing its user. For example, a callee could see the caller's name and affiliation before answering. It is a standards-track IANA registration.

plainLanguage.summary: Link a phone number to a digital business card so you can see who is calling.

questions: how does enum link phone numbers to vcards
how does enum point to a vcard
subtitle: Registers the vCard Enumservice so a phone number's DNS entry can point to an electronic business card.

tldr.problem: ENUM maps E.164 telephone numbers to URIs through DNS, but there was no registered way to say that a number's URI leads to a vCard describing its user.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the Enumservice "vCard" (type "vcard", no subtype) for the "http" and "https" URI schemes, so an ENUM record can point at a plain vCard.
tldr.outcome: A client can fetch the vCard before, during or after a call, for example to show a caller's name and association. The RFC stresses that this links numbers to personal data, so access controls matter. RFC 6118 updates it.

today: RFC 4969 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6118. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
E.164 Number Mapping (ENUM) uses the Domain Name System to refer from E.164 telephone numbers to Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs). Services that can be used with ENUM must be registered, and the process is described in Section 3 of RFC 3761.

A vCard is a transport-independent data format for information about an individual, in effect an electronic business card. vCards are most commonly sent as email attachments or published on web servers, and most popular personal information manager applications can read and write them.

An ENUM record using this Enumservice identifies a resource from which a vCard for that number could be fetched. A client could use it to update a local address book, for instance a Voice over IP phone fetching vCards for inbound and outbound calls and showing them with the call journal.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone numbers can be looked up to find web addresses. This RFC adds a new kind of web address: one that holds a digital business card.

sections.title: The Enumservice Registration
sections.content:
The registration template gives the Enumservice name vCard, the type vcard and no subtype. The URI schemes are http and https, and the intended usage is COMMON.

The functional specification says the resource identified is a plain vCard according to RFC 2426, which may be accessed using HTTP or HTTPS. Clients should expect access to be restricted, and the comprehension of the data provided may vary depending on the client's identity.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC fills in a form that gives the new service a name, says it uses web links, and warns that you might not always be allowed to see the card.

sections.title: Example Record
sections.content:
The RFC shows a NAPTR record in a DNS zone. The service field is E2U+vcard, and the rewrite rule replaces the whole input with a web URI that points to a vCard file.

The example number's domain is under e164.arpa, which is where ENUM places telephone numbers as reversed digits.
sections.plainLanguage: It is one line in the internet's phone book: for this phone number, the business card lives at this web address.

sections.title: Privacy of Record and Resource
sections.content:
The security considerations of ENUM itself (Section 6 of RFC 3761) apply. Because DNS is a public database, anything in an ENUM record must be considered public, and copies could survive after the entry and the referred resource are removed.

A URI can reveal who owns a number, for example one that contains a person's name, location and company. The record itself need not hold personal data, since it only points to a place where access could be granted. Records can also be provisioned on purpose by the domain owner, so the link between a number and an entity could be bogus unless identity verification is in place, which is out of scope.

vCards usually describe individuals, so linking a number to one gives a reverse lookup from the number to its owner. Publishing such personally identifiable information is covered by data-protection law in many legislations, and explicit consent is usually required. Users MUST consider carefully what they put in the resource and in the record.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can read the phone book, so do not write secrets in it. Even a web address can give away a name, so be careful what the card shows.

sections.title: Access Control with HTTP
sections.content:
Using HTTP lets the vCard resource reuse built-in authentication, authorization and session control. Digest Authentication could challenge requestors, and the server could build a vCard based on the client's identity or refuse access. This suits private ENUM deployments, such as within enterprises. Even public deployments could tailor a vCard to the client, for instance a social network site giving members more complete vCards than anonymous clients, based on cookies.

If access restrictions are deployed, standard HTTP authentication, authorization and state management mechanisms (as described in RFCs 2617 and 2695) MUST be used to enforce them. HTTPS SHOULD be preferred if the mechanisms are prone to eavesdropping and replay attacks.

Deployments that also use DNSSEC should consider Minimally Covering NSEC Records to prevent zone walking, since the personal data in vCards is a rich target.
sections.plainLanguage: The website holding the card can ask who you are first and show different cards to different people, like a receptionist who gives out details only to people on a list.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The memo requests registration of the vCard Enumservice according to the template in Section 3 and the definitions in RFC 3761. It defines no other registry or procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks the keeper of internet lists to add one new entry using the form in Section 3.
